Perfume rating 4.26 out of 5 with 12,761 votes

Coco Eau de Parfum by Chanel is a Oriental Spicy fragrance for women. Coco Eau de Parfum was launched in 1984. The nose behind this fragrance is Jacques Polge. Top notes are Bulgarian Rose, Coriander, Peach, Jasmine and Mandarin Orange; middle notes are Cloves, Rose, Mimosa, Orange Blossom and Clover; base notes are Amber, Sandalwood, Opoponax, Tonka Bean, Civet, Vanilla and Labdanum.

GooseWithAGrudge 11/10/25 18:15

The past several months, on my way into work, I’ve been stopping by the fragrance section of the store and giving myself a nice spritz of Chanel Coco on the way in- the first time I did it, much to the alarm of the very young sales clerk, who told me “oh… ma’am… that’s an old timey perfume, maybe you should try something else?” But I wanted to see what it smelled like, sprayed myself with it, and then went about my day. The whole time, I kept getting the greatest whiffs of a spicy peachy floral all day. While I don’t own this beauty yet (I will within the next few weeks), it seems like every time I mooch a tester spray I get compliments on this lovely scent from the most random assortment of people (from my dad, who usually hates perfume, to the tire store guy who absolutely wanted to know what I was wearing so he could get it for his girlfriend, to the cranky older lady client who usually has nothing nice to say about anyone).

It is quite strong, with pretty good silage. Lasting power is 10+ hours. I see some people down thread who are disappointed that reformulation made this one weaker- I feel like if this was any stronger it would be a nuclear level scent!

DalyDose 11/03/25 14:09

I love this fragrance without reservation- in any form, and on any person. And yes, my 35 year old self has encountered some crazy looks/comments from the astonished SA at my department store when I said I was going to purchase Coco and would like a sample of Opium, not Black Opium, but Opium. She actually looked at me, rolled her eyes, and said: "those are so loud, and dated, you might as well get Clinique Aromatics Elixir too" to which I let her know was on my wishlist, and then I sarcasitically remarked: " I like people to smell my fragrance before I enter the continent...".

It is also to be noted, I have worn Coco on and off since sneaking into my mother's bathroom at 15 to get a few spritzes, had my own many bottles throughout college, and returned to Coco as a woman in my 30s. It remains one of if not THE MOST complimented fragrances I have ever worn. I receive these compliments from friends, family, strangers, co-workers, previous suitors, neighbors down the hall from me, men of all ages, and customers when I managed a Chanel Counter who would buy the fragrance on the spot or follow me through the store to ask me what gorgeous scent I was wearing and then purchase it.

Coco is at the height of femininity and masculinity at the same time- it's just so brilliant and elevates the wearer and those lucky enough to experience Coco on the wearer in any occasion/setting.

hpaige11 11/01/25 17:14

I just bought my first bottles of the modern Coco Toilette and a vintage Coco Eau de Parfum splash, still sealed. I tried the toilette first and wrote a harsh review of it, as I couldn't understand what "boss lady" everyone was raving about. To me, it smelled very feminine and young and like an uplifting, sweet floral. Coco is much better when the weather becomes gray, damp, and chilly. Both are very much sweet florals, but with warmth from those spices seeping through. The toilette is sweet and turns dusty and a little powdery in the dry down, pleasantly so. The perfume is warm and dry, with less sweetness in the dry down, at least from what I can pick up. I do like that they last longer than some of my niche perfumes. My son likes it, too, along with Acne Studios by Malle (his favorite) and Petit Cherie by Goutal, two others that are effervescent with those sweet fruit accords. This may be sacralage, but the toilette seems to layer nicely with others.

Also, this has been written off for a long time as a "dated" perfume, but it is still very much wearable and pretty, so if you like vintage, look into it.

Mwils 10/31/25 11:28

I always avoided this because of the old lady stigma it has....my loss because it's beautiful. Stick a niche label on and it would sell like hotcakes! It's spicy, tonka, softly floral. The edt is all spice with some freshness, so much spice it tickles my nose, slightly masculine. This is those same spices initially but immediately start to settle and tonka takes lead. Within minutes I get hints of deep rose. Compared to edt this is better blended showing more of it's notes and it's lighter wearing because the edt has louder spice. Definitely not too heavy as many say. A beautiful spicy floral. Ever changing, sometimes throwing spice, sometimes sweet tonka. I get just the slightest touch of powdery on my skin not a bomb as some experience. Sexy, grown up. I'd guess 30 ish if they like classy scents and any age after that. If you like super spicy or you're male. ...get edt. If you want the spice but hints of all notes, more feminine, get edp. For when to wear I think day or night, office, at home, outings, anywhere but a bit much for medical environment. Any season except summer. It reminds me of something Tom Ford would produce.

The opening is soapy, balsamic and spicy. The drydown is a syrupy, resinous Coca-Cola. A little goes a long way, and the longevity is eternal, lasting through showers. The patchouli is so well blended as to be undetectable through the wear, as only Chanel can do.

darspls 10/13/25 03:52

To me, coco is like the younger, brighter, girlier sister of no5. It still has that fresh, soapy laundry smell, but it's not so overpowering and serious; it works alongside all the other beautiful notes in this fragrance. LizaJane 10/07/25 10:40

The older I get, the more I fall in love with this fragrance. I purchased my first bottle of Chanel's Coco in my early 20's. At the time, I was drawn more to gourmand, almost sickly-sweet fragrances, but I desperately wanted a more "grown-up" scent to wear to work or for special occasions. So, I chose Coco. I always thought she was lovely, but I don't think I fully appreciated her—until now.

I probably wore her only a handful of times after purchasing my bottle. For the most part, she sat in a cabinet collecting dust. But one evening, as I was winding down and getting ready for bed, I decided I wanted to drift off surrounded by a beautiful fragrance. I didn't have a particular scent in mind, but my hand naturally gravitated toward Coco.

The first spray floored me. Oh my GOD—she was stunning. I was met with a beautifully complex rose, paired with a subtle fruitiness I couldn't quite place. What truly grounds the fragrance, and makes it a showstopper (in my opinion), is the base of amber, sandalwood, and tonka. This combination makes Coco a bit more wearable and balanced, as opposed to the screechiness I fear she'd have without it. I couldn't stop inhaling her that evening, and as I drifted off to sleep, I felt wrapped in warmth and beauty. Since then, I haven't been able to get enough. In fact, I'm wearing her right now.

For those concerned with performance, I can confidently say Coco hold up beautifully. She has incredible lasting power, and the sillage is just right, not overwhelming, but enough that I catch whiffs of her throughout the day. I haven’t received any compliments on this fragrance, but I understand that she may not be for everyone—and that’s perfectly fine. I wear fragrances for myself, and if someone thinks I smell like an “old lady,” that’s alright. I think I smell divine.

MademoiselleMaya 09/12/25 06:48

My first contact with Chanel was Coco Mademoiselle but as time has passed I explored the brand offerings and was intrigued by the classic Coco. Because it is the inspriration behind the modernization to Mademoiselle and because it is a historical Chanel and so unique. Nowadays I like to wear event scents I am in the mood for and not necessarily my fav scent all the time.
Coco was too retro for me, and still is but I am ready to explore its many facets.
So, I requested this for my birthday since Coco Mademoiselle was also a birthday gift many years ago.
It is rather an evening scent. Sharp and spicy and retro. Cloves dominate on my skin but the background shines many facets which I like.
The parts are not that easy to recognize.
I feel amber and rose. And coriander and a bit of peach. This is the symphony after 4-5 hours.
I like the way it stabilizes on my skin and gets softer. I always have the impression that there is also an aldehydic flash in the blend. It is radiant but dark.
Winter and autumn will fit the scent perfectly.
I feel very grown-up and underdressed in it. It is a classy companion and that is undeniable. I will be learning it and hope we will fit together.
In style this reminds me of Obsession by Calvin Klein which my mother-in-law loves. She updated to Libre after a change to Black Opium Intense which she also loved so now I feel I will remind her of her Obsession with my Coco :)
So far my favourite classics that I have are N°5, Nahema and Mitsouko. Coco is fighting to take a spot on the podium.
It mellows to rose and orange blossom with spicy tinge.
I feel sharp and edgy in it.

It is a scent of a wealthy lady, standing beside you in an elevator, heading to her penthouse apartament. Article of Italo Pereira, see above
and written just now, with the goal to give a more perfume-technical review: with Chanel's Coco (1984) a masterpiece of perfumery came into the world. Jacques Polge is a genius, as is his son Olivier. I vividly remember the perfume within the 'pack of Code 4 Perfumes' which I all loved. Coco brought some hauteté to this irreverent group, a mysterious aura that, according to Karl Lagerfeld, presented an "Orientalisme Chanelissime" to the already asphyxiatingly heady perfumosphere of the 1980s. Coco wouldn't be caught under just one moniker. it is an Ambre perfume, an Orientaliste, reminiscing to Chanel's lacquered Screens in her le Ritz Appartment. these sophisticated and antique Screens (and in Asia Antique means 200 years old instead of, here, 100 years) coveted a 'Coromandel' scenerie. "There are many types of engraving on lacquer but the most popular one in Europe is known as "Coromandel laquer"." often the scenes depict exotic birds, flowers, Asian landscapes. the perfume Coco has a delicate as also very layered richness that holds all of these aspects with the help of resins and civet. Roses, Clover, Cloves, the resins with Labdanum and Tonka beans give off a very opulent and satiated with pollens Cloud of Mimosa, the said Clover, the Roses and Jasmin (Chanel's Duette) while also Orange Blossom makes sure not only the initial whiff of the perfume is dense and billowing but also lends it a lasting talent for perseverance of ...
Beauty. Karl Lagerfeld said her Orientalism came from off Venice. but of course Karl had the vitriolic tongue but also the genial insight to present his then Muse Ines de la Fressange to be the face of this fabulous and astral perfume. she was an Argentinian-French model with lianious démésure and ditto legs, with a chiseled face and intense and sweet eyes. raven black hair and clothed in the Chanel Deux-Pieces she layed on a Chaise-Longue before the Coromandel Screens in mme's Apartment in the le Ritz above (or across) 31, Rue Cambon. the Eau de parfum came first, later the Eau de toilette. but the decade asked for les Gestes étourdissantes, éblouissantes, spectaculaires, époustouflantes. and the perfume brought such stellar glamorous entrance all to the publique. Roses, Peach (a Chanel Classic) and Mandarin Orange appeared at the first stage, with Coriander seeds (of which I once read, and have sensed, that they smell like mandarins) and the Jasmin at once in the top notes (as also the first onslaught of Roses). quickly they are accompanied (or annexated) by more Roses, Cloves, and I would say I remember how it smelled then, the Mimosa and Clover. being an Amber perfume,
and 2 years after one of the most memorable (and still) Amber Perfume of all times she had a back-up in Calvin Kleins Obsession (1982) yet it wasn't the case these perfumes fought with each other. they just toxified an entire Warehouse and you walked between
the Cosmetic Isles as on Acid, hovering on LSD and Cocaine. these perfumes made a thick wall of Indole, Damascenone, Civet(one), flowers like whole guirlandes and orchards but all with the quality 'On Steroids'. plus with the Exceptional Quality. Coco shall always be a part of these Hooker Perfumes (Poison, Giorgio, Obsession, Knowing, Moschino, Gem, First, Opium, Must de Cartier et cetera) but contributed by giving them a Chanel Lift and Chiquified the decade. with (still No5, with Giorgio Beverly Hills "Red" ('wearing 'Red', everything else pales'), Beautiful, C'Est la Vie de Christian Lacroix, Boucheron, Jaipur, Tiffany and so on. this was my decade and Coco was the queen.

sensationseeker 04/08/25 11:42

Coco is a serious, complex fragrance that also has the polish and synthetic/perfumey radiance of a contemporary mainstream scent. It’s a combination I’m not used to; it’s as if a senator somehow also turned out to be a person with real integrity & competence.

It opens with sharp, bitter orange peel and glossy aldehydes, which sweeten with swoony orange blossom and amber, and a bit of a sharp hissy brightness from the coriander. A few minutes in I get achingly tender May rose, and the beginnings of a little sweet-spicy clove-and-amber thing; this is technically a spicy oriental, though I find the spices more muted.

The drydown is fantastic; ambery and animalic, edgier than modern feminine scents usually get, with the hot breath of labdanum and tang of civet.

Coco is very dressed up, very female executive or politician, but also warm and slightly raunchy and a hell of a lot of fun. There’s slight Christmas vibe from the orange/clove combo, and a happy wickedness from the civet. Coco is someone I’d want to be my mentor. I can picture her laughing with a drink in her hand and telling me all the industry inside baseball.

Let me reveal the advantages of being a middle aged woman:
You have your own money;
You love your career;
You play with your children, laugh and dance like a child;
You no longer people please;
You’re no longer sexually inhibited;
You do what you want;
People are attracted to you but random men no longer tell you to “smile”;
You have beautiful silver streaks in your hair and a no bullshit attitude;
You’re ready for Coco Eau de Parfum.

Of course anyone can wear this perfume, at any age! But there’s something deeply satisfying about wearing it when you’ve stepped into your personal power, and for me that is middle age. I tried it unsuccessfully in my twenties, then again in my 30s. Wearing it felt like wearing fancy dress. You need a certain amount of life experience to wear this authentically. Now in my late forties it fits like a glove. Whenever I want to feel confident, beautiful, warm and unbreakable, I wear Coco.

My most recent perfume purchase and a bit of a surprise.

I really thought I had gone through the classic / department store lineup of Chanel perfumes and decided that n°5 was the only one I liked. I’ve always felt that n°5 holds such a complex vintage beauty, while their other scent ranges like Chance, Gabrielle, etc. are a bit too modern for my taste / a bit generic smelling IMO.

Same went for Coco Mademoiselle, and I guess I never really looked much into Coco EDP as I just assumed it was under the same umbrella and would be similar.

I tried Coco one day though and found it intriguing, a few tests later and my nose was hooked. Coco is another vintage Chanel gem that stands out like n°5, but this time in all-out 80s attire. I’m only 22, but this perfume is undeniably 80s to me. It makes me think of heavy blush, teased hair (and the smell of hairspray), Valentino, shoulder pads, Isabelle Adjani in full glam, the cover of Rio by Duran Duran, red lacquered nails and elegantly smoking in a dark nightclub… so fun!!

It’s a bit cold and sharp, almost angular ? Maybe I’m just thinking of shoulder pads again.

I get a peachyness, interpreted in an 80s perfume peach kind of way. It definitely reminds me of hairspray, in the best way possible. Spicy and floral, I definitely can smell rose in here too. It feels baroque while maintaining a very classic Chanel DNA.

[24.08.2024]

Well, as a man I have never worn Coco EDP, but as a perfumery passionate, I can confirm it is an amber genius from another era. I will remind myself the smell of it to be more precise and than will write maybe some review.

[09.09.2024] update

Smelling this, you can easily feel the style of the formula. This perfume has an old-school, 'vintage like' character, what you can connect with the period of 50-90s smelling this blind without knowing this is Coco EDP from 1984. You can't really compare it objectively with modern French perfume projects. Telling what is "better" Jazz from 60s or Pop from 2000s doesn't has any sense xD, you know what I mean... . I find it quite fascinating, how everything is made in the chemical synergy. It's not hard to guess that it has gone through many reformulations, however, there is lots going on inside the bottle, in my opinion. It seems to be built upon 1 generation Musks (Musk Ketone, Musk Ambrette), there is also Musk Xylene, but this is banned to use in cosmetic industry, because this stuff is used in production of explosives like TNT. Why 1 gen. Musks? - they give lots of powdery facets, especially with Ionones, Vanillin and its derivatives, Coumarin as well. It is very powdery, sweet, has some subjective amber sparkle feeling to it. Some clean fractions of Patchouli also come to mind. I detect some animalic facets in trace. There are lots of spicy and rosy elements coming through as well. Some top notes like Terpenes are quite high, especially Linalool, Linalyl Acetate or Ethyl Linalool -> you can find some of them labeled on the back of the packaging, I don't know which exactly because I haven't looked on allergens xD haha. Seems quite generic to name something labeled on a fragrance while describing it right? I can smell lots of Linalool or its softer artificial version Ethyl Linalool inside the fragrance. These are quite common raw materials in classic French perfumes.

Generally, you receive balanced, sweet, powdery Amber being fresh and lively and smoothly blended with everything else in the same time. This perfumer really knows how chemistry works, fascinating once again.

I am not surprised, that opinions are quite controversial. This EDP goes very far from modern trends and taste of social majority. It can be outdated or immoral and always irrelevant for you. A big big question of preferences.

Do I like it? Yes. I appreciate this in the way like a well written book, really well made wine or painted portrait. Not in the way I would apply the fragrance on the skin. I rock modern formulations of YSL Kouros EDT, so nothing strange I like it xD. This epoch just speaks to me. Fair play to people who like "old school" perfumery times, me too.

This is strongly feminine and elegant, to my nose ofc...

I’ve loved Coco ever since my then BF bought it for me as a gift in the late 2000. It wasn’t the one I’d hoped to get and at first I felt dissapointed. But after a little time went by it grew on me and it’s been my signature ever since.
I always thought Coco as a very linear scent, very powerful right from the start. No apologies!
That’s been one of my favourite things about it. No empty promises in the opening… only for the spray to dry down into an all consuming cheap vanilla GREEN ZOMBIE MONSTER musk attack like the story goes with so many of the fragrances on the market that’s come and gone. 🧟
Coco will be
right by your side
from start to finish.

Or at least I thought so.

The new formulation from the colour of the liquid to the scent itself seems like a stranger. It feels like Chanel had given away the original formula to someone who just started in the fragrance industry to experiment with it. Like all the Chanel in the Coco was only that written on the label.

Opening is way too soft, almost like a boring painting picturing some random garden somewhere with cheap ill fitting frames, hanging on the wall of an abandoned house. It reminds me a bit of the Chanel No5 flanker Eau Premiere from the beginning of 2010. That scent I actually like but I don’t want it messing my holy Coco experience.

The new Coco continues to appear feeling uncertain of it’s purpose. Too scared to go anywhere.
Then it changes, still walking on a tightrope the middle notes may finally be revealing where the scent is heading to… Mosquito repellent!
Fly away classy
die away with flies.

The middle passes on to the base still a bit shaky and then the dry down.
Slowly you recognise the old friend.
It’s there but it’s not the same. Just a faint, frail figure waving from afar. Apologisizing it’s weakness.
Saying:
”I did the best I could.”
You almost feel sorry for it.

But then you remember who’s behind all of it.
”Like really Chanel???! Is this scent right here really absolutely the best you can do???!!!”

I don’t think so.

My old bottle I just finished was from some 2008 patch. It was perfect.
I got the new one as a present from a very important person ❤️
Things change I know.
Cosmetics and stuff you put to your skin and occationally inhale to your lungs should be as safe as possible. The use of ingredients harvested from the fellow living creatures on this planet to make fragrances should be banned yes.

So may this be my fairwell to old Coco.

Bye bye.

And a warning to you all old school Coco fans.
Do not get your hopes up,
The old Coco eau de parfum is dead.

This current one you should embrace as something knew. Maybe I too learn to love it.
But I’ll always remember the old Coco as something unique I truly and with all my heart adored.

You will be missed.

evavidal62 01/27/24 07:38

I have the expensive pure parfum (dab on) bottle from the Chanel store. But I also have the one in this picture the EDP spray. This spray cost between 100 and 300 dollars at both the Chanel boutique and the Macy's perfume department but so worth it because it is such a masterpiece of perfumery and among the best the house of Chanel ever formulated. Jacques Polge concocted this beauty at the same time he was creating Diva for Ungaro. There seems to be more going on than what the Fragrantica note for note pyramid tells us. Coco opens with what to me feels like typical classic Chanel perfume top notes - aldehydes (in this case very soft and subdued, but as bathy and soapy as the aldehydes in Chanel 5 and 22). I also detect the citrus notes of orange, mandarin and orange blossom. The citruses are zesty, bright and refreshing. Above all, the orange blossom sings. The perfume is already off to a sweet start; a soapy quality, an orange and then a peach. The peach is not too strong but it's there and quite similar to the soft peach in Arpege (Lanvin). My nasal association with Arpege is also enhanced with the note of rose (twice) Bulgarian rose and rose absolute. The rose notes keep this fragrance leaning feminine. The roses are not the main accord but they are in the background keeping this in a powdery body. There are wisps of white florals such as jasmine but mostly gold, yellow, champagne & orange colored flowers come into play. I am smelling yellow mimosa which mixes well with the orange blossom. There also appears to be a note of ylang ylang. Gorgeous. The florals are lovely; soft, powdery, sweet and like specs of gold or a shower of gold. Cloves and spices are also within the heart to base period so after the sweet floral accords you are treated to spices, but not heavy spices. This is meant to be sprayed lightly and not to be overdone. If sprayed too much, this is an atom bomb with flowers and musk. The dry down comes around and it's basically a musk but there are other notes in there that are gorgeous to discover - amber, vanilla, labdanum or rockrose, resins, spices and sandalwood. Once the florals take a backseat, the scent becomes both powdery and spicy. This perfume is hard to put a label to. It is not a full-on Oriental but has some Oriental vibes particularly the amber-vanilla musk at the dry down and finish; it's a floral and has the feel of an aldehyde floral but it isn't. It's got a luxurious Baroque quality to it, like something a royal princess or queen would wear in the Renaissance era. Think Catherine de Medici. This powerful perfume lingers for hours and has a very comforting, cozy, and warm effect. It's great for fall and winter. It smells like being wrapped up in warm vanilla and musk. I think this smells great sprayed on a faux fur coat (like on the coat) or a scarf. I wear it to girlfriend night outs on the town. It's a bit too mature for a date but smells wonderful when women are around me. This has no age but it's florals and musk keep it in an over 30 age range. However if you are in your 20s and have experience wearing vintages, especially Diva by Ungaro, or perhaps to a degree (to my nose) original Salvador Dali perfume, then this fragrance will definitely suit you. It is for an independent and intellectual intelligent and classy woman. It's for fancy dinners and to go to museums with. I absolutely love it. I recommend both the pure parfum and the EDP spray.

I want to fill up an Olympic-sized pool with it and swim a 1500m freestyle event. Buy a sensory deprivation tank and spend hours floating in the dark, just Coco and me. I don’t know why it happened. Hormones? Dysosmia? Seasons? I have no real explanation, I just know that it did.

I like to retry my “dislike” fragrances every once in a while just to see if my feelings about them change, so on a recent trip to the perfume counter, I did just that with the Coco EDP tester. I dismissively sprayed it on the back of my hand and went about my business. A few minutes later I was standing at the register waiting to pay for a purchase, and I was suddenly swept away by the scent of orange, clove, and amber. I wasn't sure where the scent was coming from at first; I only knew that I had to have it.

I looked around to see if anyone was standing near enough to smell, or if something else was being sprayed. Then I reached my hand up to my nose and realized it was me. It was Coco EDP. Confused, I left the register to spray my other hand with it. I needed to confirm this was what I was smelling because it was so different than how I remembered it. The Coco in my memory was a powder-bomb — but THIS Coco was all opulence, warmth, and sumptuous spice.

So I bought a bottle, and I’ve been wearing it every day since. That powdery facet is still present, but it’s not the lead. It’s just a fluffy, musky, pillow for the sultry, spiced fruits and rose to rest on. On a paper strip I think Coco smells a bit vintage, but on skin, it doesn’t come across dated at all — just sophisticated, warm, and seductive. It makes me want to smoke clove cigarettes and paint my nails bright red. My clothes are already mostly black, but if they weren't, this perfume would make me want to wear all-black.

I’m not sure how this will play out in the summer. It’s cold here now, the perfect weather for this type of scent. It’s hard to imagine Coco in hot, humid weather. What will I do when summer comes? Is the EDT a viable option when it’s warm out, or will I have to wait until autumn comes back around to enjoy Coco again? I guess I’ll find out in a couple of months.

rene.saller 12/08/23 20:55

I wore Coco EDP in my early 20s, not long after its release, and I loved it with a singular devotion, until I ran out of it and never replaced my bottle. I haven't smelled it in decades, but something came over me recently, and I felt a strong urge to start wearing it again--not as my signature scent but just every so often, when I want to remind myself of the person I was when I wore it to the exclusion of all other perfumes. I always loved fragrance, even as a toddler, but this was the first expensive grown-up perfume that I chose for myself (even if I sweet-talked some ex-boyfriend into buying it for me). Now I am a married lady of a certain age, and I can afford to buy a little bottle of Chanel for myself every so often. I just hope the reformulation lives up to my memories of the 1984 version. I'm trying to remember why I chose it in the first place, when I was in my early 20s, and I think it must have been that delectable Shalom Harlow 1920s-looking ad campaign, which ran in Vogue and Glamour every month back then. What can I say? I was and remain a simpleton. It's just fortunate that I picked an iconic fragrance, even if I did it for the worst and most shallow and basic of reasons. I look forward to finding out whether that clove-kissed rose is as radiant as I remember. If you can't go home again, and you can never enter the same river twice, at least you can sometimes catch a faint whiff of a beloved fragrance that conjures up a younger, quicker (but dumber), sharper-sensed version of yourself.

Update: Wearing it today, I'm getting faint glimpses (Proustian Lite) of the Coco I remember, but I can't tell if the reformulation is weaker or if my nose is simply different--it doesn't smell quite the same to me, but my frame of reference has changed a lot since then. I have smelled many other fragrances, including classic vintage scents that inspired Polge, including Diva, the fragrance he made the year before Coco, and now I'm smelling it in that context. It's a wonderful scent--a clove-kissed rose, with peach and amber and mandarin colluding with mysterious clean balsams and a rich floral vanilla--but it doesn't make me feel like I'm 22 years old again, the kind of person who needed this fragrance to feel like a real grown-up. Now I wear fragrance mostly for myself (although I prefer to wear ones that my husband doesn't actively dislike--saintly of me, no?), and I think I'll put this one on when I want to enjoy a gorgeous scent bubble. It's not a time machine, but that would be a lot to expect from 50 ml of EDP, even a Chanel.

Update: The drydown really is glorious. It occurred to me that I might actually have a much sharper sense of smell now, in my relative dotage, than I had when I was a pretty young thing because back then I smoked cigarettes, a habit I kicked for good more than 17 years ago. I suppose back then I must have smelled like Coco and Camel Lights--yick!

I'm going to add this to the regular fall rotation. Damn you, Chanel (and Guerlain): Why must you flaunt your superiority so flagrantly! What is it about your snobby French asses that render my other perfumes common and cheap by comparison? It can't just be the branding (or can it)? But wearing this is making me seriously consider confining my collection solely to the perfumes I love as much as this one, and that would mean getting rid of 80% of my collection. Too drastic, surely, but the alternative is knowing I could be wearing this (or Samsara or L'Heure Bleue or Nahéma) when I am wearing a "like" and not a "love." I suppose most people would save their best scents for the big occasions, but I mostly just wear scent at home, where I also work, so it's immaterial to me. I'm not really into this obsession for the compliments.

Coco Eau de Parfum just makes me think of the 1980's and big power suits, perms and the smell of ash trays in a gentleman's club. This stuff is STRONG! Not good at all in my opinion or particularly feminine.

I don't smell the fruity notes or any of the floral notes in the opening, but I do smell the strong and spicy smell of coriander that just WHACKS me in the face! It's quite overwhelming and not particularly subtle or pretty smelling. From the get-go I don't like this fragrance and it kind of reminds me of an Indian spice shop.

This impression of mine continues into the heart notes with me being overwhelmed by the very spicy smell of cloves that smells very heavy handed. This is at least softened somewhat by a powdery and succulent red rose and a honey-sweet clover, probably my favorite part of this fragrance. I really wish that I could smell the other floral notes in the heart though. It would have made this perfume softer, prettier and more feminine.

The very heavy and vintage smell unfortunately continues into the base, with the smoky smelling tonka bean, pungent and fecal smelling civet and the powerful and leathery labdanum being mostly responsible for this foul and mature smelling scent. The spicy and sweet balsamic oppoponax and resinous amber give this strong, sticky smell to the base too that I really don't like and the sandalwood is so strong and woody, that it makes me feel like I have been hit on the head with a wooden floor board. The only solace that I get from all of this is a nice, sweet and warm oriental vanilla in the dry down that is admittedly quite lovely.

I get fall and winter vibes from this fragrance and feel like it would be worn during the evening/night time. It would be much too much during the day. I'd say that this perfume leans masculine too and I don't think it would suit a woman to be honest, as contrarian as that may sound. It's just too woody and too spicy for that.

Sillage on me was quite big, since it projected 6 feet away from me. This fragrance lasted a long time on me too, (unfortunately for me) clocking in at around 10 and a half hours.

Despite its great sillage and longevity though, I can only really give Coco eau de parfum by Chanel a pretty bad 3.5/10. Just too mature, too smoky, too spicy, too woody and too masculine for this lady!

Coco EDP begins with what my nose perceives as rose and clove scented tobacco, an immense sillage, dark and seductive. I was daring enough to apply six sprays and I am enveloped in its plushness and envision the softest velvet, colored sepia, draping over me, like a smoking jacket. My fingers trace the leather bound books on an enormous shelf, I look out the window and see a topiary. I realize the glasses I am wearing tea shades, like John Lennon would wear. I hear a distant piano playing Gymnopédie No. 1 by Erik Satie.

Okay, sorry, I guess that's what folks in olden days called "getting lost in reverie." I suppose that's what Coco does for me, it's a "lost in reverie" sort of scent. Of course, it's a matter of perception, as I've pointed out countless times before. We can look at Coco as the premiere Chanel fragrance of 80s affluence and all the imagery that's tied to that, but that's been repeated over and again and I think we've read enough of that interpretation. What really strikes me is another review I read that mentions that it was the signature scent of someone's grandfather. Imagine that! Gender norms be damned, he smelled it, he loved it enough to wear it, and that was it.

Coco can be just as much a patriarch as it is a matriarch. It can feel like a pat on the head, a loving embrace, but in all its florals-baked-into-resins, gauzy, smoky cloak of amber glory, it can also become that precious gem you otherwise can't afford. In fact it could convince you that a physical gem, as dazzling as it may be, isn't nearly as satisfying as an olfactory one that makes an indelible imprint.

And I know people talk about Guerlinade but I feel like Chanel does its own thing, that something that makes its fragrances insanely smooth so that the top blends into the middle into the drydown seamlessly. HannahRosesAreRed 06/28/23 11:53

One of the quintessential fragrances of the 80s, preferred for the sophisticated set that wanted to make an impression without going down the Dior Poison route. This is a ladies' fragrance, plain and simple. This is a scent for confident adults–it evokes red nails, burgundy lipstick, fur or leather coats, pencil skirts, shoulder padded blazers, back-seamed stockings and high heels.

It's a bold blend of warm amber and cozy spices. Think wintertime or holiday spice candles, with a hint of cosmetic wax and animalic funk. The clove and vanilla come out the strongest, just backed up by rose and tonka bean. The coriander note adds this odd, funky hint of herby green-ness. I was worried when I saw the notes, since civet can smell pungent and garbage-y even at the best of times, and coriander (cilantro seeds) sometimes has that ammonia stentch. However, they're surprisingly understated here, and add to the skin-scent quality of the drydown. I think the creamy, earthy sandalwood helps, too.

It's a bit too serious for my taste, and the animalic notes aren’t the best matches for my skin chemistry. But this is a respectable fragrance that captures the best aspects of a certain mindset of a bygone era–but can still work today. Best for evenings or cooler weather.

Subhuman 04/28/23 13:19

For all that Chanel parade their vaunted company history at the drop of a pillbox hat, they seem to handle their perfumes from a more brisk, business-first perspective – keep things fresh, keep them modern, and keep them moving. They routinely fuss over the formulae of their classics, and not only for regulatory reasons, it seems to me. Chanel can do what Chanel wants, of course, but I am led to wonder just how much of the original fragrance resides in any given bottle on their counters. The Coco eau de parfum I first smelled over a decade ago was itself already a trimming and tweaking of the 1984 original, probably just the latest in a long line of such adjustments. I could surmise at the time that Coco likely smelled at least somewhat different in its original form, and the modern-day version bears out the same conclusion for me. I’ll take what I have, but I wonder…

All that said, Coco EdP - circa 2023 - is beautiful. Unlike some of its oriental forebears, with their lead-dense resins and balsams stomping the ground in gravitas, Coco is a rather buoyant affair. (I wonder...) It opens with orange blossom, plum, bright rose and frangipani, bolstered by woody aldehydes and a dusting of talc. The frangipani is the attention-seeker here, lush and sweet, and colorful drapery for Coco's oriental framework. (Is there such thing as a "tropical oriental"?) Jasmine, cinnamon, a brief fumbling of cloves before IFRA slaps Polge's hand away, and a coquettish opopanax join the party, followed by a very creamy amber. Soft patchouli, sandalwood, and well-heeled musk round out the finish.

In typical Chanel style, there’s a lot of a lot, blended to blurry perfection, but its ‘80s provenance makes Coco a little more legible - and loud - than some of Chanel's earlier classics. Still, I think it’s sufficiently fresh for the Sephora crowd. No rumbling retro musks or evil toxic mosses; an overall feel of shimmering powder. Of course it's elegant and polished to a gleam, but in a less buttoned-up, coiffed-hair way than you might expect from an old floriental; you can dress it up or down instead of reserving it for nights at the opera or whatever it is people who wear the Chanel that's not from a bottle do. Coco isn't a groundbreaking blend, but it’s guileless, pretty, and warm, and sometimes that's all you need.

____

TL;DR: I don't know what Coco EdP smelled like in the '80s. I know that now it smells like a chic woody floriental, exotic to no one but lovely nonetheless, and classically styled without feeling like a museum piece. An eminently wearable luxury. (Black dress and Rum Raisin nail polish optional.)

Coco is just really, really pretty to me in a very classic way. Yes, this is warmly amber and roses, but it isn't a green rose. It's dry and nearly smells a little...fusty? This gets criticized sometimes by people who aren't decidedly *into* fragrance (friends or family you would take to the mall) as being a "grandma" perfume, and that makes me a little sad honestly.  It's not vanillic, fruity or modern, it lacks white musk and it isn't *clean*, but I've never found it difficult to deal with or wrap my head around. I've smelled it many times and I've taken mental notes.

It's not overly animalic, I personally find Obsession to be stronger on the civet by a good deal (and I still love Obsession).

I don't get most of the notes here and never have, it's a spiced amber and rose to be with a dash of skank...that's it. It's not overly complex at all, but I will say that the spice has never seemed like an overdose of cloves either. It's just vaguely spicy (or my nose isn't that honed).

One time I went without wearing perfume on the way to dinner with my husband, but opted to spray this at the mall beforehand (restaurant was attached to the mall). ATTACK OF THE GENDER-BENDER

Being a rose-lover, not even Coco's iconic status as a "symbol of feminine class" could keep me away for too long.
The weird thing is that this was one of those magic elixirs a woman could use to seduce me. I was very nervous about even approaching a Chanel counter to sample a female Chanel fragrance, of all things. But diving deeper into perfumery changes things. When I tested this the first time (mid-2010), I brought a female acquaintance with me.

I totally understood why the saleslady who sprayed me was perplexed. A middle-aged woman with a conservative look, she had probably NEVER seen a man want to sample Coco for himself. Well, Coco settled and everything that would have made me putty in a woman's hands was absent. Was my nose playing tricks on me? I asked my acquaintance for a straight-up opinion. She LIKED it on me... I took a mental note of that but was still afraid to buy it and wear it. I still remember that scent haunting me for that whole day. That has haunted me for a whole year.....

Fast-forwarding to the present, I am now a proud owner of Chanel Coco EDP. I recently tried Coco again, was enchanted again and finally decided to man up. I would STILL love to smell this on a woman and it's probably still that magic elixir that the right woman could use to seduce me. But on MY skin, this is PERFECT! Roses, spices and smokey incense take center stage. Longevity is insane and the sillage is STILL outrageous. I love this enough to wear it, regardless of the perceptions surrounding it. Why? Because I love it.

In today's perfume trends, where cavity-inducing gourmands (especially vanilla) and watery florals are the norm, Coco could pass for an extremely sophisticated masculine/unisex.

For those of you who might be wondering, "How dare he?!?", I must state that Coco Mademoiselle passes for a fresh aromatic unisex fragrance on my skin. This was recently the general perception of an all-male staff.

The power of skin chemistry. The power of Chanel...

Let me reveal the advantages of being a middle aged woman:
You have your own money;
You love your career;
You play with your children, laugh and dance like a child;
You no longer people please;
You’re no longer sexually inhibited;
You do what you want;
People are attracted to you but random men no longer tell you to “smile”;
You have beautiful silver streaks in your hair and a no bullshit attitude;
You’re ready for Coco Eau de Parfum.

Of course anyone can wear this perfume, at any age! But there’s something deeply satisfying about wearing it when you’ve stepped into your personal power, and for me that is middle age. I tried it unsuccessfully in my twenties, then again in my 30s. Wearing it felt like wearing fancy dress. You need a certain amount of life experience to wear this authentically. Now in my late forties it fits like a glove. Whenever I want to feel confident, beautiful, warm and unbreakable, I wear Coco.

I had to return to review this fragrance a second time. Before, I mentioned being a bit put-off by the almost agressive rose-amber-clove accord in Coco EdP. My first impression was of something sharp and synthetic, an olfactory manifestation of the hairspray and cherry coke ambiance of the ‘80s. Paradoxically, Coco also garnered me several compliments from strangers who smelled it as they passed me in a hallway. So, I’ve felt pretty ambivalent about her for a while now.

Tonight, though, I was feeling a bit lonely and chilly, so I doused myself in Coco after a hot shower right before crawling into bed to read a book. Something magical happened, in that way particular to the alchemy of fragrance, where a scent you think you know well morphs into something altogether different. Perhaps it was the heat or the moisture, or simply a different attitude of mind, but what I smell now is a smooth and luscious creature glowing with a muted light. The rose is deep and crystalline, the clove adds luminosity and spice, and the amber—heavy and ornamental—carries them both, the brazen tone of a dense gong resonating outward in concentric circles.

I am, without a doubt, falling for Coco. People have called her the perfume of confident women, but in my experience, she requires a reciprocal warmth and vulnerability in order to open up and bathe you in her own enveloping heat. Not elegant, exactly, but certainly mysterious and unexpectedly tender. Lacking in the diaphanous quality of most of Chanel’s other offerings, Coco has a most curious drydown: a faded rose, dry, floral, fruity, and a tad soapy.
